frameworkCheck.title: AP U.S. Government and Politics Course and Exam Description (effective Fall 2026)
frameworkCheck.how: The 60 numbered CED topics (1.1–5.13) were read from the topic pages of the current PDF on AP Central, and each is matched to the StudySprint topic whose guide section and questions teach it. The CED's 13 required foundational documents and 14 required Supreme Court cases were read from its course framework (pp. 25 and 30) and are named in the unit guides where they apply. Its five skill categories (Concept Application, SCOTUS Application, Data Analysis, Source Analysis, Argumentation) were also checked: the CED says multiple-choice questions assess the first four and that no multiple-choice question explicitly assesses Argumentation. The Fall 2026 Clarifications and Corrections (https://apcentral.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/ap-us-government-and-politics-course-and-exam-description-clarifications.pdf) add four required documents (the Emancipation Proclamation, Federalist No. 39, the Gettysburg Address, and core principles from Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations), which the current CED already lists.
frameworkCheck.weightsSource: the AP Students course page and the CED's exam section (shares of the multiple-choice score), both checked 2026-11-14
frameworkCheck.examFormat: From the AP Students exam page and the CED (3 hours, digital in Bluebook): Section I, 55 multiple-choice questions in 80 minutes (50% of the score): about 30 individual questions plus sets of typically two to four questions on quantitative data (five sets), text-based sources (two sets, one with a foundational document), and visual sources (three sets). Section II, 4 free-response questions in 100 minutes (50%, 12.5% each): concept application, quantitative analysis, SCOTUS comparison (a non-required case compared with a required one), and an argument essay. StudySprint practice is multiple-choice only, with individual questions and stimulus sets; written-response practice uses College Board's released questions.
requiredDocuments: The Constitution of the United States (including the Bill of Rights and subsequent amendments)
“Letter from a Birmingham Jail” (Martin Luther King, Jr.)
Core principles from Adam Smith’s The Wealth of Nations
requiredCases: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969)
New York Times Co. v. United States (1971)
Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010)
differences: The AP Students page's unit topic lists are summaries; the CED's 60 topics are the required content and are listed per unit as framework topics.
Some topic titles appear split across columns in the Course at a Glance PDF text; StudySprint records the topic-page titles as printed in the CED.

StudySprint's data stimuli are labelled hypothetical; the AP Exam uses real data sources. Foundational-document excerpts are quoted from the public-domain texts printed in OpenStax American Government 4e.

Federalist and Anti-Federalist views on central government and democracy
Separation of powers and “checks and balances”
The relationship between the states and the national government (federalism)
How federalism has been interpreted differently over time

officialTopics: The structures, powers, and functions of each house of Congress
